newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages walk free to tumultuous reception.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages walk free to tumultuous reception.

text.p: When the first bus came out, a piercing cry came out of the crowd.
"Daddy! Daddy!" the young Asian girl, perched on a man's shoulders, shouted as she recognised her father.

Immediately microphones were thrust up to her face and camera lights trained into her tear-filled eyes. Too excited to speak she shunned her moment of fame and ran off for her first paternal hug for six nights.

More than one thousand journalists, family members and curious bystanders had assembled in the narrow leafy street of the middle-class San Isidro district to greet the 225 hostages released by Marxist Peruvian guerrillas late on Sunday night.
Hundreds of police and firemen, on permanent guard outside the residence, struggled to contain the crowd as it surged to meet the newly-freed men.
In the jubilant atmosphere, cameramen lost sight of what they were filming, sharpshooters lowered their rifles and stared. The rest clapped, cheered or cried.
"It's amazing. I just had to come here to see," said Juan Carlos Blanco, who lives nearby.
Every vantage point -- car roofs, walls, even trees -- was occupied, mostly by cameramen.
Dozens of firemen in bright red jumpsuits linked arms to open a way for the large blue buses.

Slowly, other buses followed. Dishevelled but dignified in the same elegant suits they had worn to Tuesday evening's cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's home, the freed men grinned and waved and gave thumbs-up signs.
Close by, three girls huddled together around a hand-held television, their faces stained with tears. "I can't see him. How many buses are there? I can't bear it," one sobbed.
A friend of the family sharply reprimanded photographers training their lenses on another "human-interest" angle.
"Please don't. If it was your father in there, you would understand," he said.
By the time the last bus left, crowds were lining the short trip to the police hospital waving Peruvian flags and cheering. Cars honked their horns in support.
Back at the residence, the excitement had died down, the crowds had gone and gloom was creeping back by the early hours of Monday morning.
"This is far from over. They've still got 140 people in there," said one U.S. photographer as she settled down to continue her vigil outside the residence.
